methodological_rigor.justification: The study leverages a large, well-characterized observational cohort (CCGA, NCT02889978) with 5,639 cfDNA samples (2,849 cancer, 2,790 noncancer) and establishes an empirical limit of detection via a dilution series with 7–26 replicates per contrived methylation level, yielding an LoD95 of 0.0081 and strong linearity (R=0.97). Analytic choices are defensible — Fisher's exact when counts are small, chi-square otherwise, 95% exact binomial CIs via Hmisc, and Pearson correlation for TMeF vs cfBRCA1meth. Key weaknesses: no power calculation is reported; the pan-cancer comparison tests cfBRCA1meth enrichment across 15 tumor types without any explicit multiplicity correction (nominal P-values are reported); and the TNBC/OvCa correlation samples (R=0.68 and 0.65) are small (sample sizes implied by the 17 and 14 positive cases), limiting precision. The authors explicitly acknowledge that LoD95 of 0.0081 may miss ultra-low constitutional cases detected by ultradeep PBC NGS, which is appropriate.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter observational case-control cohort (CCGA), consistent with Oxford 2b. Clinical relevance is substantial: cfBRCA1meth is positioned as both a non-invasive constitutional risk biomarker (relevant to TNBC/OvCa screening and hereditary risk pathways) and a quantitative tumor-burden metric that could guide therapy in BRCA1-deficient cancers (PARP inhibitors, platinum). Endpoints are biomarker-level rather than OS/PFS, and translational utility is demonstrated but not clinically validated for decision-making, placing it short of practice-changing. The novel sex-bias confirmation and prostate cancer depletion also open hypothesis-generating avenues for population risk stratification.

reporting_quality.justification: REMARK was applied as this is a biomarker prevalence/association study, though STROBE elements are also relevant for the observational cohort frame. Reporting is strong: pre-specified assay thresholds (4 methylated CpGs, ≥1 informative fragment), explicit LoD95 derivation, clear patient counts and demographic breakdowns (Table 1), analytic software versioning (R 4.3.2), and transparent handling of subgroup analyses. Gaps include no participant flow diagram, no formal multiplicity correction documented, limited reporting of inclusion/exclusion in detail beyond the parent CCGA citation, and no explicit REMARK checklist. Data availability relies on the parent CCGA trial registration (NCT02889978) and the public TCGA/Xena resource; raw cfDNA sequencing data are not stated as deposited in a public repository, and analytical code is not referenced.

novelty_literature.justification: The main novelty is methodological-translational: demonstrating that the GRAIL targeted methylation cfDNA assay (originally for MCED) can quantify constitutional and tumor-derived BRCA1meth in the same assay across a very large pan-cancer cohort. Several key findings — enrichment in TNBC/OvCa, sex bias in constitutional BRCA1meth, lack of strong age effect — confirm or extend prior work by Lonning, Nikolaienko and colleagues (refs 5, 7, 11), making the empirical contribution incremental rather than first-in-class. Genuinely new observations include the prostate cancer depletion signal and the correlation of cfBRCA1meth with TMeF-based tumor burden. Positioning in the literature is thorough and prior comparators are directly acknowledged without over-claiming.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly structured with a well-motivated introduction, concise methods, logically organized results, and a discussion that interprets rather than restates. The abstract is self-contained and quantitatively grounded (LoD95 0.0081, 4.1% noncancer prevalence, 15.2% TNBC, 13.9% OvCa, sex comparison P=.016). Figure captions are standalone-interpretable and specify statistical annotations (R, P, 95% CI, significance stars). Minor issues: occasional dense sentences in the Methods (e.g., LoD and dilution description), and some P-value inconsistencies between abstract (P=.001, P=.014 for TNBC/OvCa) and results text (P<.001 for both) that would benefit from reconciliation.

key_strengths: Rigorous analytical validation with empirical LoD95 of 0.0081 derived from a dilution series spanning 0.0003–1 methylation fraction with strong linearity (R=0.97)
Very large and well-characterized CCGA cohort (2,849 cancer, 2,790 noncancer across 15 tissue types) with concordant TCGA tissue-DNA cross-reference
Clinically meaningful dual utility demonstrated: constitutional BRCA1meth detection for risk assessment and cfBRCA1meth-TMeF correlation for tumor burden quantification in TNBC/OvCa
Confirmation of sex-biased constitutional BRCA1meth prevalence in the largest cohort reported to date, plus a novel prostate cancer depletion signal corroborated in TCGA
key_concerns: No multiplicity correction reported for the pan-cancer enrichment testing across 15 tumor types, risking inflated type I error for secondary findings
No power calculation and small positive-case numbers underpinning the TMeF correlations (17 TNBC, 14 OvCa), limiting precision of R=0.68/0.65 estimates
LoD95 of 0.0081 is coarser than ultradeep PBC NGS (≈0.001), potentially under-detecting constitutional carriers, as the authors acknowledge but do not quantify the resulting undercounting
Minor numerical inconsistency between abstract P-values (P=.001, P=.014) and results text (both P<.001) for TNBC/OvCa enrichment
No explicit data/code availability statement beyond the parent CCGA trial registration and public TCGA; raw sequencing data deposition not described
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a methodologically solid, large-cohort biomarker study with clear translational relevance but incremental empirical novelty building on prior Lonning/Nikolaienko work; it fits a tier-2 oncology venue (JIF ~10–19) with minor revisions to address multiplicity, data sharing, and reconciliation of P-values.
